utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Praljak. Could you try to express in words the area of Sandzak, because when you say "there," that's all that we find in the transcript. It's not very informative. Please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the east border of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the Republic of Serbia. There is a province which is called Sandzak. It is on the western borders of Serbia towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, or looking from Bosnia and Herzegovina on the eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards Serbia, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to lift an ambiguity, could you tell us whether Mr. Halilovic was born in Sandzak? Can you tell us if he stayed in Serbia would he have been a Serbian citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a citizen of Serbia. But today, as far as I know, and I believe myself to be well informed, all Muslims who lived in the territory of Yugoslavia today call themselves Bosniaks save for those who remained Muslims and actually acquired the nationality of another nation. So in Croatia you have Muslims who are Croats who profess the Islamic faith, and you have those whose religion is Islamic, and they call themselves Bosniaks. There are about 60.000 of them in Croatia and as part of national minorities, they have a representative in the Croatian Sabor, in the Croatian Assembly, which is a directly elected representative, not a part of the party's slates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to be very clear, Sefer Halilovic is born of parents that were of Muslim faith. So he was a Muslim, but he could have acquired a Serbian citizenship because he is born in a Serbian region; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's right, Judge Antonetti. He could have been a citizen of Serbia and declared himself to be a Bosniak, because Sandzak they also declared themselves to be Bosniaks by ethnicity. I know that you do not have this in France because there a national is the same as a citizen, but here you can have a national of the Republic of Croatia, who is a Czech or a Hungarian, or a national of the Republic of Serbia, who is a Bosniak or a Serb, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I had stopped you, interrupted you, and we were at page 336 when I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here again it is stated that Sefer used to say that Izetbegovic was a traitor of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Bosniak people; and that in the view of Sefer Halilovic, Izetbegovic should have resigned. For Izetbegovic, Sefer wrote that he was a graveyard digger. That without Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he dug that and so on and so forth. So he meddled. He meddled in all sorts of things. He wanted to be the political and military boss of Bosnia. He wanted to conquered it with his forces, and he had territorial ambitions in a word. Let's go to page 342 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0467. That's the Croatian, and English, 3D41-0131.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To continue, here he says that Sefer did not even like any Bosniaks if he thought them some competition to himself, and he thought so about his war colleagues and comrades in arms, Vehbija Karic, Suljevic and others. How they didn't know anything. They were ignorant. They were a burden to him, et cetera; so this was not only Izetbegovic that he had a such view of but also his own high officers in his own army staff, and he told these kinds of stories about them as well. So this was a state of total disarray. Let us go to 344 and 345.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In English it is still the same page in Croatian 3D41-01 -- 0468 and 3D41-0131 for the record, Your Honours, in English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Muslimovic testifies that there was a major difference between Halilovic and Sefer in the intellectual education and moral and every other respect, which of course is true. And we will all agree with that. I had an encounter with Sefer Halilovic. After the war in a TV duel and I can testify and it lasted about an hour or so. I can testify to the intellectual levels of Sefer Halilovic. Furthermore, he reiterated how many times Sefer had told him that Izetbegovic was not up to the task, and he quoted how many times in 1992 and the second half of 1993 he had heard Sefer say that Izetbegovic is an old fool saying stupid things. Let us go to 346 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0470 - that's in Croatian - to 3D41-0472. And in English 3D41-0132 to 3D41-0133.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Sefer, after his replacement or the replacement, sought to soil, besmirch Delic, Izetbegovic and others as much as possible. And he goes on to say that he employed the media, that he wanted to be a political and military leader of the Bosniaks, that he printed posters with his image on them, and also badges with his image on them. And I had the opportunity to see those posters myself. The great warrior smiling down on people in his poster in the pose of a victor. And then he goes on to say all the sorts of things that he did to Mr. Ahmet Tabak in order to force him to state how Izetbegovic, Cengic, and Alispahic were criminals, that they were stealing money, that they were war profiteers, and then he describes this incident, this torture. Then the gentleman goes on to describe how Sefer actually incited conflicts in Sarajevo and how he helped Caco and Celo, which are the nicknames of commanders of brigades in Sarajevo who were obedient to no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Prosecution renews its objection to this book and this testimony on relevancy grounds. I don't see how this bears any connection to either the crimes charged in the indictment or the joint criminal enterprise that's alleged in the indictment as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can be associated because Ramiz Delalic, "Celo" is referred to here, who was later involved in the action at Grabovica, which is in the area of Herceg-Bosna and is to the north of Mostar and which is in the area where there were conflicts between the ABH and the HVO. Of course this is only an appendix to all the reasons already adduced previously by General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated in the indictment, for instance, that the document of the 15th of January, 1993, which was generated in agreement with Izetbegovic was an ultimatum of the HVO which actually brought about conflicts and set in motion an avalanche of attacks by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it not clear from this text now who in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually revoked Izetbegovic, cancelled the document that he had approved, that he had produced in Zagreb together with the co-chairmen of the peace conference? Is it not clear from this book what Sefer and the rest thought -- think about peace and the agreements of peace? Is that not one of the main counts of the indictment that the HVO, namely by that ultimatum injured or hurt or -- them or caused the war with the Bosniaks? If that is not so, I don't know what I'm talking about. So please bear with me, Your Honours. Let me finish this part which I'm still working on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, yes, finish, but finish briefly, please. We understood what you're trying to demonstrate you seem to say that Halilovic has his own agenda. Maybe he was even playing a double game. And he took part in the Geneva conference because he signed a document with Mr. Petkovic. The document was -- has already been admitted into evidence, and you believe this is important to understand what exactly happened on the field. Fine, but then, on the other hand, I'm sure you understood Mr. Stringer. He was speaking about the crimes and your responsibility when it comes to these crimes, or alleged crimes; so please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not losing sight of that, Your Honours. I know what I did and what I signed and cannot be -- there's no way that my association with any crime can be proved in any way whatsoever except by idle stories, constructions. One of those constructions is the 15th of January. And we lost and wasted hours and hours of time on that, but nobody said why that fell through and who was behind it. But just these two documents were taken as such. Let me, therefore, say very briefly it is here on pages 334, 350 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 352 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm a bit amazed. You come here as a soldier. Of the one the first duties of a soldier is discipline, and normally it applies to all ranks, and discipline implies self-control, and I'm surprised that you seem not to be able to control the speed -- the speed of your speech and have to be admonished once per hour about after -- this is the fourth week that you're doing it. So if you want to show that you have some discipline and self-control, this is the way you could very usefully do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not -- I was not asking you a question. I was telling you how you should behave usefully in your own interest as a witness, and that's all. That needs no comment from you. Please, Ms. Pinter, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I do not agree with the concept of how a military should behave. A soldier has discipline, but the mind works in different ways. Judge Trechsel has the right to present his view on the army or how a drill soldier looks like. I'm not a drill soldier. I'm a human being, a man; and I'm doing my best, my level best, but the concept of a such a drilled Prussian soldier, Prussian idiot, is something that I will not accept, even if it does come from His Honour Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm sure you misunderstood my fellow Judge, and I would like to take the floor on this point. My fellow Judge reminded you that on several occasions the Trial Chamber asked you to slow down. You've understood this and you have apologised for speaking too fast. My fellow Judge added that a military man because that's -- I mean, you were a general. We have to keep this in mind. So normally a military man is self-disciplined. It's part and parcel of a military man, and it's a essential quality for anyone in the military. This is what he wanted to point out. If a Judge is, therefore, asking you to slow down, you must obey. That's all there was to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise, and I'll really trying, but before I became an active-duty serviceman, I was a director for 25 years, which means that you have to be dramatic, thespian; and you know, Your Honours, that it's a different kind of formation of a thought of speech, so I'm really trying; but please understand me, this is my second nature coming out, my important part of myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but we are not -- we're not talking to someone who was a director, who was a director. This is not the director we're speaking to. We're talking to the general here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So the page numbers are 3D41-0473.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To 3D41-0477 in Croatian and 3D41-40 -- -0134 through 3D41-0137.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have this and another portion. This is a brief description of the role of Sefer Halilovic in supporting some of the commands who are listed here, and the brigades so that they ended up subordinate to him and no one else, and how those units blocked any kind of action which probably Mr. Izetbegovic tried to carry out in order to introduce some kind of order into the town of Sarajevo; and there was a great deal of disorder and chaos there, and it's a well-known fact. People know that. And we have some details that are recounted here from the fact that Sefer ordered that anyone who wants to pose them should be fired at into the body and there were conflicts between the MUP forces and the police with Caco and Celo's followers, and people in Sarajevo know that. This problem was solved as you will see a little bit later. Let us move on to page 358. That's the last portion of this book that I want to use.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To 3D41-0482. In English that's 3D41-0137 through to the end.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is about the arrest of the members of the 10th Brigade. And the command of the military security in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina has to send a letter to some commanders warning them that they are no longer a part of the military organisation, that they are out of -- out of control, that they're no longer controlled by any military or political factors. And then he goes on to say that Mr. Izetbegovic gave a positive assessment to the perseverance on Muslimovic's part to solve the problem with Caco. He speaks about how those people stole gasoline, took people away to dig trenches, and so on. And then he goes on to say that Celo's and Caco's men, and those are two brigade commanders that are at issue here, arrested some 20 members of the civilian police, the military police, and officers of the BH Army. They beat some of them up. And when -- attempts were made to solve this and President Izetbegovic was involved in that too. He spoke to some of Caco's men. Caco is one of those commanders, and Caco's men, of course, issued an ultimatum for the release of some of his men or they would shell the Presidency building. President Izetbegovic vacillated. He couldn't make a final decision. And then President Izetbegovic received some people from Caco's brigade, and these talks were very hard for him. The negotiations were very hard. The president had to replace Muslimovic and another well-known commander, Hajrulahovic, Talijan, at the request of Caco's men. And it goes on to say that that night Caco set up combat lines along the streets of Sarajevo. And then on the 3rd of July, 1993, he corralled some 200 people, rounded up some 200 people in the streets, including Admir Delic, General Delic's son, and President Izetbegovic was forced to decide to release from the Pecara prison the people who had been arrested, the people who belonged to Commander Caco. The situation then calmed down. I have nothing more to say about that because this book speaks for itself, and it is quite clear. It's a clear image of the other side, the side that the HVO was supposed to create, a joint state, a joint army, arm them. And that's what we were doing actually. Thank you very much. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Our next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document we've just seen, I'd like to put you a question. I'll will address later on your relationship with Mate Boban. We will see this in detail later, but as a military commander, whether it be Mr. Halilovic, you, yourself, Mr. Petkovic, General Mladic, we can mention a number of names, but as a military commander, I want to ask you this: Is a military commander placed under the command of the acting president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, absolutely. A military commander may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your answered by saying yes. How can you explain on the basis of the documents we've seen a few moments ago that relate to Halilovic that's being replaced by Delic, and that a coup d'etat is being prepared? Izetbegovic is not respected. How can you explain this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the explanation, Your Honour, is very simple. As Mr. Izetbegovic had not prepared for the war and the people of Sarajevo, the people who -- in the street, Caco's, Celo's men and those who belonged to others, were the first to grab hold of weapons, and they saved Sarajevo. They were the first to fight the Republika Srpska army. They manned the position. They fought. They got killed. And that is now they grew in stature. And it takes a year and a half. It took one year and a half. It was only in the fall of 1993 that Mr. Izetbegovic managed to arrest all these people and introduce order into Sarajevo. So from what I know, there is not a shred of doubt that the inclination of President Izetbegovic was to resolve the situation. But if he arrested Caco and Caco has a brigade composed of his pals, there was no structure. They would simply leave the positions and Serbs would enter Sarajevo. His hands were tied. He had to bide his time for his organisation, for his army to grow in strength so that he could finally grapple with the criminal elements. He did not have a state and then created an army. Izetbegovic and the Presidency survived because Caco's men and Celo's men and Juka's men went out onto the positions, and those were street urchins so to speak, and they have had their own ideas of morality. Those were people who had their share of -- and that is why this happened. The armies that defend the state, it's difficult. It takes time to turn them into a proper army because they say, Well, this is my rifle. I defended this patch. Who are you? And you say, I am the president of the state, and he just waves you off. What kind of a president are you? You can't pay his salary, you didn't recruit him, and you cannot punish him, you cannot discipline him. If you discipline him, there goes your town. You lose your town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a question to the initial question of the President, namely whether generals are submitted to the president of the state. This you answered positively. You said yes, and I think it's even more obvious if the president of the entity, I'm avoiding now the word "state," of the entity is also the supreme commander of the military. How can you reconcile this with what you also said today, and I think previously, that you accept no authority between yourself and God.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, you misunderstand me, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I am highly disciplined in this sense, but if a policy or any supreme commander issued orders or decisions to me that I couldn't accept as a human being, then I do not oppose it by staging a coup d'etat. I leave the organisation. So I did have some disagreements about the organisation of the overall life in Herceg-Bosna with Mr. Boban, some disagreements, but it never occurred to me to do what Sefer Halilovic was doing. I at that time, because the Muslim offensive ended and I was sure that we had managed to defend ourselves in this lull, I calmly asked to be relieved of my duty. And this is a completely different situation from what we have here. So in any organisation, let's say the judiciously at one point you cannot accept something. You say, All right. I don't want to be part of it. So I'm speaking about the moral sentiment to the extent at which I am prepared to participate or to be a member of something, and for as long as I am, I am very disciplined and I always abide by all the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not exactly what I had meant, but I leave it at that. Thank you. I did not want to compare you to Mr. Halilovic at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In the binder "Central Bosnia," there is a single document that I need, and by your leave I would like to call it up in e-court so that you don't have to change binders because we will go back to the -- to the book so it's 3D02873. It was submitted to everyone so just that you don't change your binders you can look at it on the screen. Now I would like to ask General Praljak -- we're waiting for it to come up in e-court and then I would like to ask him to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, it's the chief of VOS, Ivica Zeko. He was in Central Bosnia, operational zone Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I think the date is important here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the 9th of May, 1993, and at that time, and I didn't take it from the book, in the presence of General Morillon and others, the demilitarisation was signed of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, and other zones. So Sefer Halilovic, who was opposed to UNPROFOR's presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic said, yes, okay, fine, the units that we are defend -- that are defending our territory in Eastern Bosnia we will now transfer them for the final clash with the Ustasha and then we will have all routes open to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could we now please have 02648. It's Sefer Halilovic's book, "A Cunning Strategy." General, what parts would you like us to read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pages 7 and 8, and it will take us a short time to go through the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D33-0962, Croatian, and that's 3D40-0818, and 3D40-0819 .

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the 7th of July, 1993. That's when Mr. Sefer Halilovic's removal from office was in the offing, and again a -- a meeting was arranged with Mr. Petkovic in Kiseljak, in the UNPROFOR base, yet another one, and it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. This book is not in the binder books. It may be somewhere else, but it is not in this binder which is entitled "Books." And it is also not on the list of documents at the first page of the -- of this binder, at least not under the number that we were given.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken. It's 3D02648, and it is listed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now I've found it. The number given was 2 -- well, it is okay now, but it was another number first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please about ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is Sefer Halilovic's book that he wrote probably compos mentis, and there is no reason I should expect that particularly because I know all those details. So Sefer Halilovic is supposed to attend this meeting with Petkovic, but President Izetbegovic tells him no you don't have to hurry that meeting is unimportant, and in the morning we have other things to do. So you can see that Mr. Izetbegovic did not consider the meetings with Mr. Petkovic and others to be of any great importance, because he was preparing to get rid of Sefer Halilovic. At page 8, he says that he had an unpleasant conversation with General Morillon and that Ganic was there, too, and that they asked -- demanded from Morillon that the embargo be lifted, and Sefer, in fact, was very brusque with Morillon. He said remove this trash that is UNPROFOR and how yourself off [as interpreted] where you came from, and we, the BH Army, will reach a deal with the Ustasha and Chetniks about whom Bosnia belongs to. So apart from the language that this man uses, and he even reports it in the book, it is really astonishing this immense arrogant stupidity. He has 70 percent of the territory that was taken away from him by Serbs, and he claims that he has 250.000 men under arms, and he says that he will defeat them. The only thing that is needed is for UNPROFOR to go away. You really have to listen to it and wonder. Now we can move to pages 14, 15, and 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D33-0964 is the page number, and 3D0965, 66, and for the English it is 3D40-820, 3D40-821. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this first bit is quite clear. I have nothing to add. It's the proposal by the BH Presidency about the new appointments, about dismissals, Sefer Halilovic and Rasim Delic, and just a comment by Sefer Halilovic when he saw that Alija Izetbegovic had signed this on the 2nd of June, 1993, his first thought was that it had been prepared for a long time and that this it was heinous or treacherous. That's what heinous means. And says that the differences between him and the president were great, that they were two worlds not only with respect to defence and -- defence concepts but on many other issues too. And Sefer Halilovic testifies himself what Muslimovic had previously said about him and what we saw in the previous document. And now may I look at pages 18, 19, 20, and 21 to 23, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D33-0967 to 3D33-0972, and in the English it is 3D40-822 to 3D40-826.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very important text because it's first-hand testimony about how the talks were conducted on this famous problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina's division, and he speaks about the meeting with President Izetbegovic and Ganic, and he refers to him as a Yugoslav because Ganic was also from Sandzak; and he was also a national of the then Yugoslavia and would be a national of the state of Serb today. And then another observation made here is that Mr. Sefer Halilovic was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's up to Your Honours and the lawyers to explain the fact of how in an elected body, a body elected at the elections and confirmed in that way, that is to say the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how there can be some appointment or you take someone by the ear and say, You're now going to be a member of the Presidency. Well, would things like that, when it comes to things like that, and when in Croatia a body was to be established that would be more expeditious, then a national security council was set up. And it never entered anybody's head that you now, Bobetko, Praljak, are a member of the Presidency because Croatia had a Presidency too. But it's not up to me to say although I can't understand how you can appoint and nominate someone, for example, the president of France or something, the Presidency, or whatever. And then he goes on to say that -- well, he's wondering whether the people of Sandzak would accept the decision for him to move to Eastern Herzegovina so that the Serbs can come and settle in Sandzak then. Obviously Ganic, who is from Sandzak himself, would like that because that would round off his majority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he comes out in favour of what is being discussed there. Of course, Sefer does not agree, and he says that he's a soldier. And they say, All right. We know that you understand all this. And then they say, Only a fool will not change his opinion. Then Sefer goes on to explain why he doesn't agree, but he also observes that Alija said to Ganic later on, "Did I tell you that -- didn't I tell you that you shouldn't discuss this matter with Sefer?" And then Sefer keeps sticking by his guns and says it must remain intact. It is indivisible, and so on and so forth. And with respect to this same topic, there was a conversation in the plane on our way back to Geneva, on the way back to Geneva, and that was in January. So they set out from Sarajevo on the 1st of January, 1993, and now he describes how much pride there was involved, who would get -- be allowed to get into the private jet, who would take the regular flight to Geneva, and so on and so forth. So there was a lot of vanity and pride afoot there. And there was irony here, bring that Ustasha in. That was stated with irony. Sefer was opposed to this. Who was Jasmin Jaganjac in order to be able to get into that plane? Anyway, this describes an unruly atmosphere that shouldn't have been present. Now, he -- Sefer says he was taking his interpreter and body-guard, I suppose, to safeguard him from some evil Swiss. I beg your pardon, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I have to make a joke now and again. And at the end of page 21 there, let's see Sefer Halilovic's line of thinking. He left the hotel, got into a taxi. He says that they both used hands and sign language instead of speaking English, and that they were looking for the Bosnian delegation and then he understood that the Bosnian delegation was Karadzic and that the Bosnian delegation was Boban too. And the Yugoslav delegation was taking part as well there, that is to say Cosic, Milosevic, Bulatovic, and he says the United Nations palace was full of Chetniks and Ustashas, and very -- it was all we could do to find the real Bosnia and Herzegovinian delegation. And let me repeat once again, Your Honours. Those people felt themselves to be a nation. Sefer Halilovic saw himself and everybody he commanded as a supernation, the Aryans. These are Chetniks, Ustashas that have to be expelled and killed -- or killed, and he was above all that. He was a nation above, a people above, and he's going with that view to negotiations in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is time to have a break. It's 12.30. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we completed the pages about Jasmin Jaganjac and the events described on page 22. Would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sefer, in the breaks in the negotiations in Germany, he left for Germany and Turkey -- the pause in the negotiations he left for Germany and Turkey. He didn't agree with Jasmin Jaganjac role, and there was the dilemma of it would either be him or Jaganjac. And quite obviously Jaganjac left the negotiations, and from that we can see that the four months of Jaganjac's work and my own work to set up a joint command was futile. We wasted a lot of time and effort and talks and nothing came of it. It's important to mention here that the talks between Mr. Izetbegovic, who in fact recounted his talks with Mr. Arafat, the PLO head, and Mr. Arafat told him, said: "Mr. Izetbegovic, I was offered a portion of the land too -- a portion of land, too, and there is no Palestine state to this day." And he advised Alija Izetbegovic to take a part and not to call for the maximum demand of having an entire Bosnia-Herzegovina but to take what he could. And then he says to Sefer, who is against this, that he's harbouring a delusion and that a part of Bosnia should be taken which will allow the people to come back, people who had been expelled to Croatia, to come to that portion of land, because otherwise they might be left with nothing. Sefer is benevolent and says well, nobody who respects the Bosnian state is withheld any rights. The general term used is the "Bosnian state," and that term is used today, but in fact it's Bosnia and Herzegovina. And after he presented his views, Izetbegovic said that he needed a part of the land which would be big enough to take 2 million inhabitants. Some will come in, others will leave. So that would be the best solution. So that's as far as the thesis goes of who always has this idea of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina in their minds. The only question is how much who would get. Now we can move on to page 24 and 25, and I'd just like -- well, and pages 26 and 27. You can give us the proper numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. The Croatian text is on 3D33-00973 to 3D33-0977, and for the English it is 3D40-80827 -- 0827 -- 3D40-0827 to 3D40-0829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I still go back to the page 1 -- no, 3D40-0826. It was the one which was before us last. I also read here Sefer quoting himself as saying: "We do not want everything. We want to live in equality with all those who have always lived in Bosnian, without depriving of their rights anyone who respects the Bosnian state." How do you interpret this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I can see it. So the words "we do not" already puts Mr. Sefer in a position of saying how he respects or does not respect the Bosnian state. As for me, in respect of the way that Sefer Halilovic conceives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he is the one to determine who or what respects it or not is not something that I could agree to, but this could be tolerated were it not for his other statements, if we did not comprehensively look at everything that he says. So I interpret this to sound like this: If you are loyal to Sefer Halilovic and his views of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then it is all right. But if you would by any chance have any idea that would be discrepant to his, then you would not be respectful of that state. Then he would either put you deep six you or he would banish you to Croatia. That's it. I do not consider this statement of Sefer's any different from all of his other statements to the effect how the Chetniks and Ustasha should be defeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please, General, let us revert to our basic page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly in respect of all these pages, Sefer was already shown the draft document of the Presidency about replacements, dismissals, et cetera; and he was harshly protesting here saying that he was also a member of the Presidency and had the right to -- saying that the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina only speaks about the chief of Main Staff, that they were violating the law, that this was a decision that was counter-constitutional and in contravention of the law. Mr. Izetbegovic says that this is his problem and that Sefer is meddling too much in matters. Sefer also states his opinion of people -- of the people who were appointed generals. He speaks badly about Delic, bad-mouths other people as well saying that Delic did not fight and so on and so forth. So everything. What Selimovic placed in his book is confirmed in this one as well by Sefer Halilovic too, name that Muslimovic and Delic cannot be generals, that they were guilty of violations, that all of Muslimovic's activities were in the very least very disputable because all the time he spent all the time in the basement of the Presidency. So this reflects a general wholesale political and military disorganisation, disarray, and nothing more. Can we move on? Page 54 -- pages 54 and 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's 3D33-0978 to 3D33-0978 -- 9 and in the English 3D40-830, and 3D40-0831.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here Sefer is talking about misunderstandings with Izetbegovic the president of the Presidency ever since 1991 when he had hopes that Bosnia and Herzegovina would get ready for war which was imminent, which was on the horizon; and he speaks how he had organised the Patriotic League organisation as it was called at the time. He refers to how Karadzic was threatening that if the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be successful and this is what Karadzic said in parliament, he said that the Muslims would disappear and President Izetbegovic sent this message to the citizens that there will be no war in Bosnia and Herzegovina because it takes two to quarrel and obviously the Muslims did not want to engage in any quarrel, so according to his logic, because they didn't want to quarrel, nobody would attack you. Well, one really needed to be able to say something like that. Sefer was saying that as we will all know Mr. Izetbegovic maintain his neutral position also when Dubrovnik was being destroyed and during the JNA's attack on Slovenia and Croatia, and when in 1991 in September he said after the massacre and the attack in the village of Ravno that it was not their war, the Muslims' war, I guess. Also, Sefer refers to the fact -- to his intention to mobilise 250.000 people. He gives statements to the effect that he had 250.000 or so people in the ABiH army. He said that New Year's Eve in 1992, the newspaper "Oslobodjenje," he says that Alija -- Alija will not attack Bosnia and -- that the army will not attack Bosnia and Herzegovina and that in Brussels, in the paper "Le Soir," Izetbegovic actually claimed that the people were actually awakening from a couchemar, seeing what was going to be happening. And on the 17th of March, 1992, in an interview to a Croatian paper, he said that the army had changed, that it was now different in terms of quality, in terms of psychology. That's its intentions and objectives were different and that an army would not occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina and undertake a coup d'etat. In "Oslobodjenje," there was published, and we will all were familiar with that. I knew it for a fact that he had said, Izetbegovic: "Go for a walk. Look around you. See that everything is peaceful. Don't be taken in by rumours. The situation is under control. So you can peacefully walk around town." Several days after that, Sarajevo came under extremely heavy shelling that was the situation. Can we see 56, 57, 58 and 59 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry I have a somewhat technical observation to you, Mr. Praljak. It is not clear to someone who listens always whether you are telling something out of your own head or whether you are taking it from the paper that is in front of us. For instance, you have spoken about 250.000 or so people. I do not find this figure on pages 54 and 55 which are before us. I'm not going to tell you what you should say, but I am asking you to make it clear when you are saying things from your head or when you are just referring to what is in the book that you are using. Can you agree to that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. Here I invoke documents that I have already shown this Court, documents of the Patriotic League, namely, where Mr. Halilovic speaks about already having 250.000 men, and in another document where he very clearly says that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina has more than 250.000 men. These are documents that have been shown here. I am speaking here -- I'm saying here that Halilovic claims in this book everything that I in different periods claimed likewise before this Tribunal, both in respect of Ravno, both in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is attacking Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was not inviting you to comment on the substance. I just would like you to tell us when you are departing from what is in this text. You may appreciate that we are not -- have present in our mind the thousands of documents that have already been shown to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Here Halilovic says what is also my contention and which has been reiterated time and again, namely that apart from Vojvodina, namely this eastern part, i.e., the western part of Serbia, Croatia was attacked at Vukovar, that operations were launched against Croatia from Bosnia and Herzegovina and that Izetbegovic claimed that at that time while the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the renegade Serbs in Croatia was doing what it was doing, that the presence of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary and that it would be the fundamental military force of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It also says that Izetbegovic asked Croatians in Polog to let go those tanks, the tank brigade towards Kupres, and it was, in fact, let go to come at his insistence. Then it refers to the existence of the Ram plan and the academy memorandum and how everything was clear, how the intention was to destroy and to create a Greater Serbia, but Judge Trechsel, you see that part of this plan was also to destroy the Bosnian state and the Bosniaks. He does not mention the Croats here. After this perhaps acceptable sentence he says the Bosnian state. He does not say Bosnian and Herzegovina, but he does -- he says the Bosnian state, which is not the same. Furthermore, he says that the unambiguous conclusion is that the very dangerous war is being prepared, dangerous to the Bosnian people and the Bosnian state. I must say that there does not exist a Bosnia or a Bosnian nation. These are very dangerous political thesis. This is how the Yugoslav people exists as a form of the implementation of the dictatorship and negation of nations, and Sefer is using the same expressions, the same words, everything that was being said in Belgrade after World War II; so Sefer says this is Bosna, Bosnian, not Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Bosnian there lived -- lives the Bosnian nation. No. In Bosnia does not live the Bosnian nation. In Bosnia live Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs, Jews, the Roma; and there is no Bosnian nation or Bosnia people. These are these basic planks, thesis, that this is about at that I'm contesting. These theses are in his mind, unitaries -- a unitarian state in which Sefer rules. So if you are not Bosnian nation member but -- and you happen to say that you are a Croat, he has all the argumentation, just as it was in Yugoslavia, to lock you up for two or three years of gaol. Furthermore, he states that according to what Mr. Izetbegovic told the paper "Oslobodjenje" that the JNA shall be radically transformed, that it shall become the Bosnian army, and then he actually corrects himself as he's quoting, he says the armed forces. Your Honours, the Bosnian army and the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in our conditions, our conditions who -- of us who passed through this unitarianisation [as interpreted] of the country these are crucial differences. Is this Bosnia and the Bosnian nation? Or is this Bosnia and Herzegovina that can have its own armed forces? These are incredibly important differentiations, distinctions, and so on and so forth. I shall not now belabour the point why the arms were not taken -- why arms were not taken from the barracks of the JNA. That is evident. Let us now move on to pages 60, 61, and 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he speaks about how within the MUP the protagonists of the special war were hiding. This is the thesis about which His Honour Judge Antonetti asked me several times, and I said that there were hundreds of provocateurs there of those who provoke conflict, in fact. Those who were the promoters of and agents of special warfare. Now Sefer wonders how could have Juka Prazina, the well-known criminal, Sarajevo criminal, how could he have become the commander of the reserve force of the Special Police? Muslimovic on his part says that Sefer Halilovic had made that possible so that one doesn't know here who is responsible for what. Then he goes on to say that Juka, when it was decided that he should not be the chief of the police, that he was promoted and the Presidency of the state appointed him commander of the special forces of the MUP units. He wonders here, Your Honours, in particular, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, how could have Milorad Ekmecic, Slavko Leovac, Vojo Milijas, Nenad Kecmanovic, or the brother of Nikola Koljevic have left Sarajevo unhindered? Milorad Ekmecic, these are all Serbs by the way. That's one thing. Secondly, Milorad Ekmecic is a very well known historian, a professor of history, a Serb. Nenad Kecmanovic was, in fact, even -- and a brother of Nikola Koljevic. According to Sefer, these people, apart from being Serbs, were in no units, you but according to Sefer Halilovic, they were supposed to be locked up because they were Serbs and also probably also blackmail. Koljevic was to be blackmailed with his brother who would have been locked up. That is the sense of this sentence. Who made it possible for them to depart Sarajevo? Free people, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, university professors. Nenad Kecmanovic, a professor at the university, Lecic as well. I don't know about the others. This is a very sinister thesis, you know, when you read it in this way. Imagine if you read somewhere that Praljak had wandered somewhere and written had how could Muslims have left Sarajevo? How could they have allowed some wounded men to leave? How could they have allowed some Serbs to leave when they could have told him, No we're going to hold you here and then you see what you're going to do. Furthermore, he goes on to say that Alija Delimustafic, at a government session verified the decision that had been agreed with Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who was the chief of the overall KOS of the Yugoslav People's Army and how the army had protected all the TV relays and occupied them all in this way. This is, Your Honours, the answer to the question why no communication with Sarajevo was possible, why no signals could pass, why the city was completely blocked in terms of information and communication apart from the radio ham operators, of course, and certain long radio waves, probably. And they could do this because they had special communications and devices able to send out signals across the mountains. And then he says that Delimustafic had agreed with Petar Gracanin, who was the minister of the interior of the federal Yugoslav government and with Vasiljevic who was the chief of KOS, KOS, agreed upon the arrival of approximately 100 inspectors from the federal SUP, SUP, who were of course members of KOS as well who completely paralyzed the work in Defence preparations. And I would like to mention in this regard if you recall the moment when Franjo Tudjman at a meeting with Filipovic said when he was offering up secession from Yugoslavia and military cooperation and an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina without any agreements with Tudjman and when he says to Mr. Filipovic this is what I propose, but I don't believe that Mr. Izetbegovic is going to accept that because he is surrounded by KOS people. And here we have it. Here's confirmation of that, confirmation of a fact like that. Then he goes on to speak about money. I don't think we need to spend any more time on this page. It's just confirmation of the facts and the matters that I set forth and matters dealt with in the documents and which testify to how the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was forged and also how the war and the conflict and the attack by the BH Army against the HVO had instructors and helpers, agents, aiders and abettors, and how many midwives there were to produce that particular baby. Now may I have pages 70 and 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Croatian text is 3D33-0987 and 3D33-0988. The English version is 3D40-0836. Go ahead, please, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says here that Fikret Muslimovic was the chief of HOS in the 4th Corps, and that as a Communist he was in charge of Muslim nationalism at that time. And then he goes on to recount a meeting that took place in the summer of 1991 where Muslimovic stood up to Izetbegovic. He referred to him as a fundamentalist, as somebody who was trying to break up Yugoslavia, and then with his Serbs in the JNA that he would never be Alija's soldier. And here you can see that somebody who worked for KOS you can see how strong the organisation was, in fact, because this shows it all. And he says Ivan Stambolic, who was one of the top officials, top leaders in Yugoslavia, he says the weaker Tito became, the stronger and more sovereign the war minister became and that it was -- or the defence minister became and that through KOS he had complete control over the Yugoslav People's Army, its cadres, policy, and all the rest of it. And then it goes on to say that KOS did not only hold its pause over the JNA, but it had its pause over security and Serbia and says that Stambolic writes this in his work called "The Path to Wilderness" on pages 185 and 187. So KOS was an all-powerful organisation within Yugoslavia, especially after Tito's death in 1980. May I now have page number 79, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D33-0993, and the English version is 3D40-0839.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I'm going back to the sentence uttered by Sefer Halilovic that Judge Trechsel mentioned. He referred to it. Mr. Sefer Halilovic, how was it that Mr. Sefer Halilovic allowed those to be -- that he allowed people who were loyal to the state to remain there and weren't Bosniaks. Let's see what he says here. He says the SDS and the HDZ, the behaviour of the leadership of the HDS and -- HDZ and SDS, and especially the Chetniks and Ustasha units in the war from 1992 to 1995 are best evidence of persistence in the agreement to divide up Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there you have it, Judge Trechsel. The man just needed six or seven pages to forget what he wrote 15 pages earlier on. And 15 pages on, he says that the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say Mate Boban, Prlic, and the rest; and in the army, Petkovic and Praljak, they are Ustashas, Ustashas who had reached an agreement on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then he goes on to lie blatantly and says, "We never fought among ourselves." And quotes the example of Stolac and Mostar where we just happened to be. Well, first of all, the Chetniks marched in and we withdrew, and then the Ustashas marched in and the Chetniks withdrew, and that's how peace came about. And we gained Splitska Banovina to Podvelezje, this illiterate captain of the Yugoslav People's Army doesn't know that a Banovina -- the Banovina is in not in the area of Podvelezje and then he says in that Stolac, Kiseljak, Konjic, and Vares they came across Ustashas socialising and trading. Well, where are the Chetniks in Kiseljak? That's something we don't know, but I assume he knows something about that. Then he goes on to speak about something that -- well, now that you have -- well, you saw the statements made by Muslims about the fighting in Stolac and in Mostar and so on, and if you add up all the wounded and dead, the casualties in the fighting against the JNA, the number of Croats who were killed, and the number of Muslims who were killed, too, then your stomach turns when you read sentences like this from a third-rate wheeler-dealer here who not only insults Croats, but he also insults many of the reports written about the people expelled and so on. He's just insulting to everyone. That's just it, but I'm going to move on. He goes on to say that the SDA and the official policy of the state is being waged by Mustafa efendi Ceric, the one-time imam of the mosque in Zagreb. And furthermore, he says that Bosnian today looks just the way KOS, the KOS, wanted it to look like, that is to say divided up according to ethnic lines and boundaries and the Bosniak question has been reduced to the Islamic problem in Europe and he says that Muslimovic together with Zijad Ljevakovic played a key role in re-educating the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina based on exclusively party lines, a party army or, rather, that it became ideologized [as interpreted] in the religious sense strengthened by the Mujahedin or reinforced by the Mujahedin. And we can move on. Page 97 and 98.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you comment on what you have just said? May we have your comments to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you want me to comment. I think that we presented all the documents that are relevant. We've tendered them. I think they speak for themselves. They're crystal clear, and if somebody is able to speak in this way about that fighting over there, especially in Stolac and so on, and this is something that General Petkovic led and I led it in Mostar, although towards the end I was in Stolac myself; and if you remember all the dead and wounded and if you remember all those who had been expelled across the Neretva River, then, well, I can say this quite calmly, that it's something that only a fool could utter, an insulting fool, and that's what it is. But I'm in a court of law. I'm in a courtroom, so I have to stick to that but that's my cool opinion and I think I managed to convey it with a cool head. You can't even make a chicken coop with a man like that let alone a joint army, not even a chicken coop.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you were speaking about Stolac and Mostar, what year did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now we go on to page 97, which is number 3D33-0996 up until 3D33-0997. And for the English it is 3D40-0841.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just briefly. Here he says how much money was collected for the Muslims through special accounts, who had access to the money and could sign for it, and that it was an informal group from the Party of Democratic Action, but for the most part made up of people who in 1983, as the Young Muslims Movement were convicted and sentenced to terms of imprisonment. Izetbegovic, Cengic, Sabic. They were in prison. It goes on to say that that group were in fact working in Zagreb and were referred to as the Zagreb group and that they were organising volunteers coming in from the Islamic countries, and so on and so forth. I don't think we need comment on that any further. May we move on now. We're going to skip the next portion. We have dealt with that with other documents. We have orders about that operation and so on. May we have page 121 and 122 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It is 3D33-1010 to 3D33-1011. And in the English it is 3D40-0853.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says here that a military organisation has been set up throughout the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that an army has been established made up of five corps and that he managed to liberate 58 percent of the country. And he says that there he counts free liberated territory under HVO control until 1992. Well, man's lying. He's just lying, pure and simple. There's no question of 58 percent of the country being liberated, but I suppose he's allowed to do that and say that. And then he says when we in the Main Staff of the HVO and Croatian army saw that there was nothing -- that nothing would come of the Milosevic-Tudjman agreement, that they then clashed with the army and that the Ustasha units entered Prozor, but never mind. The Main Staff of the HVO and the Croatian army understood, under quotations, that Tudjman was a fool and why would he sign something like that and we took matters into our own hands and then we had nothing else left to us as but as Ustashas to attack Rama. Well there you have it, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I don't know whether this portion has been translated, whether you have the translation of it, but he claims here that the Bosnian patriots had an army numbering five corps with about 250.000 men, and I quote, I'm quoting this now: "The Bosnian patriots during that same time had an army of five corps strong with about 250.000 fighters, and it was successful in tackling the criminals on two fronts. And he goes on to say that there have never been any such examples in history that with 250.000 men he was able to tackle this other force." And then he goes on to enumerate which corps of the Yugoslav People's Army had how many tanks, armoured APCs and men. He talks of the Knin and Rijeka Corps that were, of course, in part transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then he goes on to say that the forces of the extremist part of the HDZ were organised in three brigades numbering about 6.000 men and several smaller units amounting to the strength of a company or battalion. Now, I understand none of this anymore, because in that entire area with all those Ustashas he says there were 6.000 of them and yet he has an army of 250.000 men, and they're being attacked by the Ustashas with just 6.000 men; and he's having to fight on two fronts. I don't understand any of that. It's all nebulous and incomprehensible apart from the fact that it is quite clear that an agreement with people of that kind and everything that the Prosecution said about it being a clash with -- that -- that HVO caused the clash with the BH Army and that the HDZ policy was a nationalistic policy which I assume then supported the HVO to carry all this out, well, there's not a single shred of evidence, no arguments to say that we wanted to cut off part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was the Croatian policy. That's why I claim that both these books are highly relevant for this incomprehensible -- well, to me it's incomprehensible -- the incomprehensible way in which the indictment has been constructed. And I'd just like to look at page 165 and 166, and I'll conclude with that because I don't need to deal with any more of his documents if we could just look at those two pages now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see these pages tomorrow, because with you and your counsel, I need to take stock of how much time you have. As you know, the Trial Chamber has granted you 55 hours. There is no question as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned to give you any extra time. This would be an unbalanced situation vis-a-vis the other accused who have not had any extra time. Before you testified yourself, you had one hour and 30 minutes, you then had 53 hours and 30 left. Since you are testifying, sitting where you are opposite me, you have had approximately 32 hours to be precise, 31 hours and 52 minutes. We are not going to be too picky about these seconds. Now, if I subtract these 23 hours 30 and the time you've had, as of tomorrow you would have 21 hours and 30 minutes left. For you to be able to finish and to be able to hear your witnesses out of these 55 hours, you wanted 36 for yourself. You have had 32. You would, therefore, have four hours left to finish. I have had a look at the two remaining binders, and in light of all the documents contained in these, I doubt very much that you will be able to finish in 4 hours. The Chamber is not against the fact that you go beyond your 36 hours, but that would be part and parcel of the overall time you have, i.e., 51 hours and 30 minutes. Based on that, there are a number of witnesses which you are going to call to testify. We don't know which ones are coming, which ones are not. This has not been confirmed, but this is not our problem. We have no preference either way. It's for you to tell us who should come and testify in support of your defence, but you should not overlook the fact that the Prosecutor will have exactly the same time as you have had to cross-examine you. If you have 36 hours, the Prosecution will have 36 hours. If you have 40 hours, the Prosecution will have 40 hours. So that is something you need to remember. After that, I'm fairly certain that your counsel will ask for redirect, and this extra time has to be included in these 21 hours and 30 minutes, so all this needs to be clear for you, and I'm giving you a piece of advice. So all of this unfolds in the best possible way, make sure that you liaise with your counsel. Make sure which documents you wish to adduce, and even if you don't know what the Prosecutor is going to say and which issues he is going to address, you must already think ahead and prepare for the redirect. You will not have any extra time and not have more than those 55 hours that you have been given. We don't have unlimited time. Therefore, it is something you need to be aware of. From the Trial Chamber's point of view, there's no problem. If after 36 hours you would like to have 38, 39, or 40 hours, that's for you to work out; but if you have 40 hours, then the Prosecutor will automatically have 40 hours also. So look into this. The Trial Chamber is totally prepared to facilitate your defence like it does in all cases, but it is not prepared to give you any extra time. So it's for you to work this out. You have stressed these books you have shown to us. There are the binders that address the issue of the Main Staff that may be interesting, but let me remind you we've heard nothing about the capture of Mostar, the snipers, the Mostar bridge, and so on. So you can adduce these elements any way, I just needed to let you know. I needed these few minutes to share this what you. We shall resume Mr. Sefer Halilovic's book tomorrow, because we have all afternoon and half the night to leaf through these tens of thousands of pages you are showing us. It is just about a quarter to 2.00. I wish you all a very pleasant afternoon, and we shall reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Prlic and Coric not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
